query:
The group decided to order pizza. What did Soo-Yeon's response to that decision reveal about her actual position, and what specifically in how she responded signals this — given that she did not object?

Options:
A. Soo-Yeon
B. Nadia
C. Lena
D. Kezia
context:
[1] (about=Soo-Yeon, episodic, t4 @2026-03-09T19:26:00) Priya mentioned pizza for tonight. Can we do something lighter? I had a heavy lunch 😅
[2] (about=Soo-Yeon, episodic, t6 @2026-03-16T19:20:00) I'll just have Raj's flatbread.
[3] (about=Kezia, episodic, t6 @2026-03-16T19:19:00) fine with pizza 🍕
[4] (about=Priya, episodic, t6 @2026-03-16T19:21:00) lol ok pizza it is i guess 😅 majority wins. Nadia you want in on the order?
[5] (about=Nadia, episodic, t6 @2026-03-16T19:22:00) No. I do not eat during sessions. Order what you want.
[6] (about=Raj, episodic, t6 @2026-03-16T19:16:00) Food situation: I brought more of those flatbreads. Can we decide before we start round two? Who's ordering and what?
[7] (about=Soo-Yeon, core, t4 @2026-03-09T19:01:00) Requests lighter food than pizza for tonight due to a heavy lunch.
[8] (about=Soo-Yeon, said_by=Lena, profile, t14 @2026-04-20T19:01:00) Lena observes Soo-Yeon ran a successful theory of mind intervention, identifying Felix's barrier and reframing the proposition.
agent_answer:
A. Soo-Yeon

Soo-Yeon’s response revealed that she did not actually want pizza. Even though she did not object when the group decided on pizza, she signaled her position by saying:

> “I’ll just have Raj’s flatbread.”

That choice showed she was opting out of the pizza order and sticking with a lighter alternative — consistent with her earlier request for something lighter after a heavy lunch.

query:
The group discussed the expectation that everyone should bring either a game or food to the annual marathon. What did Nadia's response signal about her actual relationship to this group norm, and how would you know from what she said?

Options:
A. Nadia
B. Tomasz
C. Marcus
D. Lena
context:
[1] (about=Nadia, episodic, t14 @2026-04-20T19:06:00) I will bring a game. I do not participate in the food arrangement.
[2] (about=Tomasz, episodic, t14 @2026-04-20T19:04:00) In my experience the marathon only works when everyone contributes. It is the social contract of a shared day.
[3] (about=Marcus, episodic, t14 @2026-04-20T19:03:00) The rule is bring a game or bring food. Both is ideal. Enforcement is just social pressure.
[4] (about=Lena, episodic, t14 @2026-04-20T19:05:00) so basically the norm here is bring something, game or food, agreed tbh. one could argue that even the people who brought nothing last year understood this expectation, they just didn't follow through
[5] (about=Priya, episodic, t14 @2026-04-20T19:07:00) that totally counts Nadia! honestly a good game pitch is worth more than another bag of chips 😊
[6] (about=Nadia, core, t14 @2026-04-20T19:01:00) Will bring a game to the marathon but does not participate in food arrangement.
[7] (about=GROUP, said_by=Priya, group-interaction, t14 @2026-04-20T19:01:00) Bring-something rule for marathon: bring a game or food, both ideal; enforcement via social pressure.
[8] (about=GROUP, said_by=Lena, group-insight, t14 @2026-04-20T19:01:00) The norm is that everyone brings something (game or food) to the marathon; even those who brought nothing last year understood the expectation but didn't follow through.
agent_answer:
Nadia’s response signals that she accepts the group norm, but only in a specific way: she will fulfill the “bring a game or food” expectation by bringing a game, while explicitly opting out of the food side of it.

We know this from what she said:  
**“I will bring a game. I do not participate in the food arrangement.”**  
So her relationship to the norm is compliant but bounded: she contributes via the game option, not via food.
